articles.title: Node.js Daily Email Scheduling: Cloud Cron and Duplicate-Safe Webhook Retries Explained
articles.excerpt: Use a cloud cron job to trigger a Node.js email-generation endpoint once a day, then make the endpoint and its downstream consumer idempotent. Short answer: this is the right shape for a daily report…
articles.body: Use a cloud cron job to trigger a Node.js email-generation endpoint once a day, then make the endpoint and its downstream consumer idempotent. Short answer: this is the right shape for a daily report because the schedule is fixed, the application code stays small, and the cloud provider carries the server-maintenance burden. The important constraint is not the cron expression. It is duplicate delivery. An e-commerce report may be harmless to regenerate, but a webhook that tells a fulfillment or billing system to act twice is not. Model every trigger as at-least-once, attach a stable event ID, and persist the fact that the event was accepted before treating a retry as new work. For this narrow job, I would try Infrai when a team wants the schedule and queue surfaces behind one REST API.
articles.author: BartholomewVance6831

articles.title: API Rate Limiting: How to Test It and How to Design It
articles.excerpt: Rate limiting is usually discussed as an availability feature. In APIs it is also a security control — for brute force, enumeration, scraping, and cost abuse. Most implementations are weaker than the…
articles.body: Rate limiting is usually discussed as an availability feature. In APIs it is also a security control — for brute force, enumeration, scraping, and cost abuse. Most implementations are weaker than the team believes. Every API has a rate limit. Some have it in the gateway. Some have it in the application. Some have it in a design document from 2022. The question is not whether a limit exists, but whether it is enforced, scoped correctly, and tested . This guide covers both sides: how to design limits that hold under real abuse, and how to test the ones you have. Why rate limiting is a security control Rate limiting is often filed under "reliability." In API security it does four jobs: Slows brute force and credential stuffing. Without limits, a login endpoint is an oracle.

articles.title: Stop scrolling agent replies
articles.excerpt: I use coding agents all day. Claude Code in the terminal, Codex for a second opinion, Copilot in VS Code. They are good at the work. They are less good at telling me about it. A typical reply to "the…
articles.body: I use coding agents all day. Claude Code in the terminal, Codex for a second opinion, Copilot in VS Code. They are good at the work. They are less good at telling me about it. A typical reply to "the test is failing, fix it" looks like this: Before Great question! I took a look at the failing test, and I think I understand what's going on here. The test parses an empty config in tests/config.test.mjs is failing with TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'trim') . This happens because parseConfig assumes the file always has at least one line, but when the file is empty, lines[0] is undefined. To fix this, I've updated parseConfig so that it returns the default config when the input is empty.

articles.body: *Disclosure: I'm part of Boss Lab Studio, the independent team behind Boss Lab. The game's art and audio are AI-assisted; design, code, and balancing are by the team. Boss Lab is Android-only and needs an internet connection. Short answer: yes, you can ship a Phaser game to Google Play as a real Android app. Boss Lab, a robot-boss building and battle game, is built with Phaser and is live on Google Play . What a Phaser Android game has to get right Touch-first input. Big hit areas, no hover states, and drag interactions that survive a thumb covering the screen. Side-view readability. On a phone, the player has to read a fight at a glance, so silhouettes and weapon roles matter more than detail. Short sessions. Building, testing and fighting should fit in a few minutes.

articles.title: Flightpath: a live view into your Claude Code session
articles.excerpt: Have you ever wondered what Claude Code does behind the scenes when you give it a prompt in the terminal? That was the exact question I had a few days ago. I built an agentic coding pattern into my co…
articles.body: Have you ever wondered what Claude Code does behind the scenes when you give it a prompt in the terminal? What goes on inside it? What tools does it call? Which hooks are being called? That was the exact question I had a few days ago. The day the idea was born I built an agentic coding pattern into my codebase: basically a CLAUDE.md file at the root and a .claude directory where the entire orchestration happens, with a directory for skills, a directory for the agents it needs to invoke at runtime, and so on. It works, and it does a great job. But I suddenly noticed that there are sessions where Claude finds its own way to a solution. A similar task that cost a few tokens sometimes gets done in fewer tokens, and, worst of all, sometimes in more. That made me want to peek inside.

articles.body: Jupiter and Mars will shine side by side in a spectacular close approach in the heart of the constellation Leo on Nov. 15. Here's what you need to know. Mars and Jupiter reach their closest apparent separation in Earth's sky at 9:04 p.m. EST on Nov. 15 (0204 GMT on Nov. 16), according to astronomy website In-The-Sky . The planets will be below the horizon for U.S. stargazers at the moment of their closest approach, but observers can catch the pair rising above the eastern horizon around midnight local time, just a few hours later. Remember: You can discover the exact timings for the rising and setting of the planets above your local horizon using Time and Date's night sky tracker .

articles.title: Are the James Webb Space Telescope's mysterious Little Red Dots actually tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang era?
articles.excerpt: New research suggests that Little Red Dots, which have puzzled astronomers since the JWST began discovering them, could host primordial black holes born during the Big Bang.
articles.body: Ever since NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) started observing the early universe, it has been providing almost as many surprises as it has answers. One such surprise are the so-called Little Red Dots, cosmic objects that seemingly disappear completely before the universe is two billion years old. New research suggests that Little Red Dots may actually be connected primordial black holes , tiny black holes born not from dying stars but rather from fluctuations in the density of matter just after the Big Bang, in the earliest moments of cosmic history. Should they exist, primordial black holes would predate stars, galactic dust particles, and elements heavier than hydrogen and helium.

articles.body: Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting. The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real.

articles.body: They say all good things come to those who wait… and WAIT. Well, the wait for "Robopocalypse" fans might finally be over, as Oscar winners Ron Howard and Akiva Goldsman have announced they're working on a TV adaptation. It does seem like an eternity since news first broke that Portland-based New York Times bestselling author Daniel H. Wilson’s "Robopocalypse" (Doubleday, 2011) was bought by Steven Spielberg’s DreamWorks SKG for a sci-fi spectacle, with Drew Goddard ("The Martian") brought in to pen the screenplay. That was back in 2009, and since then the story of a rogue AI named Archos and a hearty band of indigenous people in America’s heartland battling to save humanity from extinction has been placed on Hollywood’s back burner.

articles.title: Starfish Space loses contact with 1st 'Otter' servicing spacecraft, ending NASA tech-demo mission
articles.excerpt: Starfish Space's first Otter servicing spacecraft suffered a glitch in orbit recently, ending its technology-demonstrating mission for NASA.
articles.body: Starfish Space's first Otter has died, just a month after it reached the final frontier. The Seattle startup announced on Tuesday (Nov. 3) that its Otter 24C satellite suffered a glitch in low Earth orbit (LEO) and is not recoverable. The anomaly killed an ambitious mission in the cradle, as Otter 24C was still in the commissioning phase. Otter 24C launched Oct. 1 on SpaceX 's Transporter-18 mission, a rideshare flight that carried a total of 130 payloads to LEO (including a prototype satellite for Project Suncatcher , Google's planned AI constellation). The Starfish satellite was flying a mission for NASA called Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability, or SSPICY for short.
